options.text: The organisation of living things into groups based on their characteristics
The process of evolution
The study of how organisms reproduce
The study of cells and their functions

questions.explanation: Classification (taxonomy) is the organisation of living things into groups based on their shared characteristics. It helps scientists communicate about organisms, identify species, and understand evolutionary relationships.

questions.stem: Who developed the system of classification that uses a hierarchy of groups?

options.text: Carl Linnaeus
Charles Darwin
Gregor Mendel
Louis Pasteur

questions.explanation: Carl Linnaeus (1707-1778), a Swedish botanist, developed the hierarchical system of classification still used today. He also introduced binomial nomenclature, the two-part naming system for species.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the Linnaean classification hierarchy from largest to smallest?

options.text: Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Family, Order, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Domain, Species, Kingdom, Genus, Family, Class, Order

questions.explanation: The correct order from largest to smallest is Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Each level contains organisms with increasingly similar characteristics as you move from Kingdom down to Species.

options.text: A system that classifies organisms by their habitat
A system using one name for each organism
A system that uses numbers to identify organisms
A two-part naming system using the genus and species names

questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature is the two-part naming system where each species is given a name consisting of its genus and species. For example, humans are Homo sapiens. The genus name is capitalised, and both parts are italicised.

questions.stem: The three-domain system classifies organisms into which three domains?

options.text: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya
Plants, Animals, Fungi
Vertebrates, Invertebrates, Microorganisms
Prokaryotes, Eukaryotes, Viruses

questions.explanation: The three-domain system, proposed by Carl Woese, classifies all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. This system is based on differences in ribosomal RNA and cell structure, and is now widely accepted as more accurate than the older kingdom system.

questions.stem: Why has classification changed over time?

options.text: Because the Linnaean system was completely wrong
Because scientists keep making mistakes
Because new evidence from DNA analysis and microscopy has improved understanding
Because organisms change their characteristics every year

questions.explanation: Classification has changed because new technologies like DNA sequencing and electron microscopy have revealed evolutionary relationships that were not visible from physical characteristics alone. This has led to reclassification of many organisms.

questions.stem: As you move down the classification hierarchy from kingdom to species, what happens to the number of organisms in each group?

options.text: It fluctuates randomly
It increases
It decreases
It stays the same

questions.explanation: As you move from kingdom to species, the number of organisms in each group decreases but they become more closely related. A kingdom contains millions of species, while a species group contains only organisms that can interbreed.
